definitions.definition: A mortgage, as used in the Registration Act 1908, refers to a mortgage as defined in section 58 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, being the transfer of an interest in specific immovable property for the purpose of securing the payment of money advanced or to be advanced by way of loan, an existing or future debt, or the performance of an engagement which may give rise to a pecuniary liability. Under section 17, instruments creating or affecting mortgage interests in immovable property of value one hundred rupees and upwards are compulsorily registrable, and under section 48, a registered mortgage takes effect against any subsequently executed and registered mortgage-deed relating to the same property.
definitions.plain_english: A mortgage is a legal arrangement where a person who owns property (usually land or a building) uses that property as security or guarantee to obtain a loan from a lender such as a bank. If the borrower fails to repay the loan, the lender has a right over the property. In India, most mortgages of significant value must be registered with the local Sub-Registrar's office to be legally valid and to have priority over later claims.
real_world_examples: A farmer in Punjab mortgages his agricultural land to a cooperative bank to secure a crop loan of ₹5 lakhs; the mortgage deed must be registered at the local Sub-Registrar's office to be compulsorily valid under Section 17 of the Registration Act.

A homeowner in Mumbai mortgages her flat to HDFC Bank to secure a home loan of ₹60 lakhs; the registered mortgage-deed gives the bank a prior enforceable charge over the property against any later mortgage or oral agreement.

A shopkeeper in Chennai creates an English mortgage on his commercial premises in favour of a private lender; upon registration, the mortgage takes effect against any subsequent registered mortgage-deed on the same property under Section 48.

A borrower in Delhi executes two mortgage deeds on the same property to two different lenders on different dates; under Section 48, the earlier duly registered mortgage-deed takes precedence over the later registered one.

A landlord in Kolkata endorses a mortgage-deed acknowledging receipt of part of the mortgage-money; such endorsement is exempt from compulsory registration under Section 17(3)(b) of the Registration Act.

A company in Bengaluru mortgages its factory premises to secure a debenture issue; the underlying registered instrument transferring interest in immovable property to trustees must be registered under Section 17.
what_it_covers: A simple mortgage where the mortgagor binds himself personally to repay and agrees that in case of default the mortgagee shall have a right to cause the mortgaged property to be sold.
An English mortgage where the mortgagor transfers the mortgaged property absolutely to the mortgagee with a proviso for retransfer upon repayment of the mortgage money.
A usufructuary mortgage where the mortgagor delivers possession of the mortgaged property to the mortgagee to receive rents and profits in lieu of or in payment of interest on the mortgage money.
An equitable mortgage by deposit of title deeds in a Presidency-town (such as Mumbai, Kolkata, or Chennai) to secure a debt.
A registered mortgage-deed that takes priority over any subsequent registered mortgage-deed relating to the same immovable property under Section 48 of the Registration Act.
what_it_excludes: An endorsement on a mortgage-deed merely acknowledging the payment of the whole or any part of the mortgage-money, which is explicitly exempt from compulsory registration under Section 17(3)(b).
A receipt for payment of money due under a mortgage where the receipt does not purport to extinguish the mortgage, which is also exempt under Section 17(3)(b).
Oral agreements or declarations relating to mortgaged property, which cannot prevail against a duly registered mortgage instrument under Section 48.

Instruments relating to shares or debentures of a joint stock company that do not directly create, declare, assign, limit or extinguish any right, title or interest in immovable property, even if the company's assets include immovable property.

A document merely creating a right to obtain another document (such as an agreement to mortgage) that will, when executed, create the actual mortgage interest — such agreements do not themselves require compulsory registration under Section 17(2)(vi).
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an instrument qualifies as a mortgage under the Registration Act determines whether it is compulsorily registrable under Section 17 (making it void for want of registration if unregistered) and whether it enjoys statutory priority under Section 48 over subsequent mortgages and oral agreements relating to the same property. Failure to register a compulsorily registrable mortgage-deed renders it inadmissible as evidence of the transaction and defeats the mortgagee's security interest entirely.

definitions.definition: 'Movable Property' includes standing timber, growing crops and grass, fruit upon and juice in trees, and property of every other description, except immovable property.
definitions.plain_english: Movable property refers to any property that can be physically moved or transferred from one place to another, and which is not fixed to the earth. Under the Registration Act, it specifically includes things like standing timber, growing crops, grass, and fruit on trees. Essentially, if a property does not fall under the definition of immovable property, it is treated as movable property.
real_world_examples: A farmer in Punjab sells his standing wheat crop to a trader before harvest — the crop is movable property and documents related to it do not require compulsory registration under Section 17.
A timber merchant in Kerala purchases standing teak trees from a landowner for felling — the trees constitute movable property under this Act, and the transaction need not be compulsorily registered.
A mango orchard owner in Maharashtra agrees to sell the fruit hanging on the trees to a wholesale buyer — the fruit upon the trees is movable property and the agreement is treated accordingly.
A vehicle dealer in Mumbai transfers ownership of a fleet of trucks to a logistics company — the trucks, being movable property, are not subject to compulsory registration under the Registration Act.
A sugar mill in Uttar Pradesh buys sugarcane standing in a field from a cultivator — the growing crop qualifies as movable property, and the sale deed is not mandatorily registrable under Section 17.

An artist in Delhi sells a collection of paintings and sculptures to a gallery — these items are movable property and their transfer documents are not required to be registered under Section 17 of the Act.
what_it_covers: Standing timber — trees that have been identified and earmarked for felling and sale as timber
Growing crops such as wheat, rice, or sugarcane still standing in the field at the time of transaction
Grass growing on land, whether sold for grazing or cutting purposes
Fruit upon trees and juice contained within trees at the time of the agreement
All other property of every description that does not qualify as immovable property, including machinery not permanently fastened, vehicles, and goods
what_it_excludes: Land and buildings, which are expressly classified as immovable property
Hereditary allowances, rights to ways, lights, ferries, and fisheries — these fall under immovable property
Things permanently fastened to the earth or attached to structures fixed to the earth, which are treated as immovable property
Benefits arising out of land that are recurring or attached to ownership of land, classified as immovable property
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether property is classified as movable or immovable determines whether a document relating to it must be compulsorily registered under Section 17 of the Act — documents concerning immovable property above Rs. 100 in value require mandatory registration, while those dealing with movable property generally do not. This classification also affects the priority rules under Section 48, where registered documents override unregistered oral agreements concerning the same property.

definitions.definition: A non-testamentary document is any document that is not a will or testamentary instrument, which is executed inter vivos and operates during the lifetime of the executant, and which may relate to immovable or movable property. The Registration Act, 1908 uses this term to distinguish all living-party instruments — such as sale deeds, mortgages, leases, and gift deeds — from testamentary dispositions that take effect upon the death of the maker.
definitions.plain_english: A non-testamentary document is simply any legal paper or agreement that is signed and takes effect during the lifetimes of the people involved, as opposed to a will which only takes effect after someone dies. Examples include sale deeds, mortgage deeds, lease agreements, and gift deeds for property. These documents must follow specific registration rules under the Registration Act and, once registered, are legally binding against the whole world.
real_world_examples: A sale deed executed in Mumbai transferring a flat in Andheri from a seller to a buyer, presented at the Sub-Registrar's office for registration under the Registration Act, 1908, is a non-testamentary document requiring a proper description of the property under Section 21.

A mortgage deed created by a farmer in Punjab hypothecating his agricultural land to a cooperative bank as security for a crop loan is a non-testamentary document that, once registered, takes effect against any subsequent oral agreement relating to the same land under Section 48.

A registered lease deed for a commercial shop in Connaught Place, New Delhi, executed between a landlord and a tenant for a period of five years, is a non-testamentary document that is entered in Book 1 (Register of non-testamentary documents relating to immovable property) at the Sub-Registrar's office.

A gift deed executed by a parent in Chennai gifting a residential plot to their child, and registered at the local Sub-Registrar's office, is a non-testamentary document. If the plot lies across two sub-districts, the Sub-Registrar is required under Section 64 to send a memorandum to the Sub-Registrar of the other sub-district.

A partition deed dividing ancestral agricultural land in Rajasthan among three brothers, registered at the relevant Sub-Registrar's office, is a non-testamentary document, and a memorandum must be forwarded to each relevant Sub-Registrar under Section 66 if portions of the land lie in different sub-districts.
what_it_covers: Sale deeds transferring ownership of immovable property between living parties.
Mortgage deeds creating a charge or security interest over immovable or movable property during the executant's lifetime.
Lease deeds and tenancy agreements relating to immovable property executed between landlords and tenants.
Gift deeds conveying property from a donor to a donee while both are alive.
Partition deeds dividing jointly held immovable property among co-owners.
Exchange deeds, settlement deeds, and other instruments relating to property rights that take effect during the lifetime of the executant.
what_it_excludes: Wills and codicils, which are testamentary documents that take effect only upon the death of the testator and are governed separately under the Registration Act.
Authorities to adopt, which are treated as a distinct category under the Act and are entered in Book 3 (Register of wills and authorities to adopt), not Book 1.
Oral agreements or oral declarations relating to property, which have no documentary form and therefore cannot constitute a document of any kind under the Act.
Court decrees and orders, which are judicial instruments and not documents executed by private parties, even if they relate to property.
Memoranda forwarded under Sections 64 and 66 themselves, which are administrative records of registered non-testamentary documents and not themselves non-testamentary documents.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a document is classified as a non-testamentary document determines whether it must satisfy the property description requirements of Section 21, must be entered in Book 1, and, once registered, will take precedence over all prior oral agreements or declarations relating to the same property under Section 48. Failure to meet the requirements applicable to non-testamentary documents — such as insufficient property description or failure to attach a copy of a map or plan — results in refusal of registration, rendering the document unenforceable as a registered instrument.

Examples: A sale deed executed in Mumbai transferring a flat in Andheri from a seller to a buyer, presented at the Sub-Registrar's office for registration under the Registration Act, 1908, is a non-testamentary document requiring a proper description of the property under Section 21. | A mortgage deed created by a farmer in Punjab hypothecating his agricultural land to a cooperative bank as security for a crop loan is a non-testamentary document that, once registered, takes effect against any subsequent oral agreement relating to the same land under Section 48. | A registered lease deed for a commercial shop in Connaught Place, New Delhi, executed between a landlord and a tenant for a period of five years, is a non-testamentary document that is entered in Book 1 (Register of non-testamentary documents relating to immovable property) at the Sub-Registrar's office. | A gift deed executed by a parent in Chennai gifting a residential plot to their child, and registered at the local Sub-Registrar's office, is a non-testamentary document. If the plot lies across two sub-districts, the Sub-Registrar is required under Section 64 to send a memorandum to the Sub-Registrar of the other sub-district. | A partition deed dividing ancestral agricultural land in Rajasthan among three brothers, registered at the relevant Sub-Registrar's office, is a non-testamentary document, and a memorandum must be forwarded to each relevant Sub-Registrar under Section 66 if portions of the land lie in different sub-districts.

Covers: Sale deeds transferring ownership of immovable property between living parties.; Mortgage deeds creating a charge or security interest over immovable or movable property during the executant's lifetime.; Lease deeds and tenancy agreements relating to immovable property executed between landlords and tenants.; Gift deeds conveying property from a donor to a donee while both are alive.; Partition deeds dividing jointly held immovable property among co-owners.; Exchange deeds, settlement deeds, and other instruments relating to property rights that take effect during the lifetime of the executant.

Excludes: Wills and codicils, which are testamentary documents that take effect only upon the death of the testator and are governed separately under the Registration Act.; Authorities to adopt, which are treated as a distinct category under the Act and are entered in Book 3 (Register of wills and authorities to adopt), not Book 1.; Oral agreements or oral declarations relating to property, which have no documentary form and therefore cannot constitute a document of any kind under the Act.; Court decrees and orders, which are judicial instruments and not documents executed by private parties, even if they relate to property.; Memoranda forwarded under Sections 64 and 66 themselves, which are administrative records of registered non-testamentary documents and not themselves non-testamentary documents.

Why it matters: Whether a document is classified as a non-testamentary document determines whether it must satisfy the property description requirements of Section 21, must be entered in Book 1, and, once registered, will take precedence over all prior oral agreements or declarations relating to the same property under Section 48. Failure to meet the requirements applicable to non-testamentary documents — such as insufficient property description or failure to attach a copy of a map or plan — results in refusal of registration, rendering the document unenforceable as a registered instrument.

definitions.definition: A non-testamentary instrument is any instrument that does not derive its operative effect from the death of the person executing it, including instruments which purport or operate to create, declare, assign, limit or extinguish any right, title or interest, whether vested or contingent, to or in immovable property, as well as instruments which acknowledge receipt or payment of consideration on account of such transactions, or which transfer or assign any decree, order of a Court, or award affecting immovable property.
definitions.plain_english: A non-testamentary instrument is any legal document that takes effect during the lifetime of the person who signs it, as opposed to a will or testament which only takes effect after the signer's death. In the context of the Registration Act, this mainly refers to written documents like sale deeds, gift deeds, mortgage deeds, and lease agreements that deal with property rights and are meant to be acted upon immediately or at a future date while the parties are alive. Such instruments often require compulsory registration to be legally valid and enforceable.
real_world_examples: A sale deed executed in Mumbai by a seller transferring ownership of a flat worth ₹80 lakhs to a buyer — this is a non-testamentary instrument that compulsorily requires registration under Section 17.

A mortgage deed executed in Delhi by a homeowner in favour of a bank to secure a home loan, creating a charge on immovable property — this is a non-testamentary instrument requiring compulsory registration.

A deed of partition executed among three brothers in Chennai dividing ancestral agricultural land between them — this non-testamentary instrument must be registered as it extinguishes and creates rights in immovable property.

A lease deed executed in Bengaluru granting a commercial tenant rights over an office space for a period of five years — this non-testamentary instrument requires compulsory registration as it is a lease exceeding one year.

A deed of assignment executed in Kolkata transferring a court decree that awards immovable property worth ₹2 lakhs from one party to another — this is a non-testamentary instrument mandatorily registrable under Section 17.

A declaration deed executed in Hyderabad by a property owner acknowledging the receipt of full sale consideration from a buyer, which extinguishes the buyer's obligation — this non-testamentary instrument requires registration.
what_it_covers: A sale deed executed between living parties transferring ownership of immovable property valued at ₹100 or more.
A gift deed executed by a donor conveying immovable property to a donee during the donor's lifetime.
A mortgage deed creating a charge or security interest over immovable property in favour of a lender.
An instrument acknowledging receipt of consideration for the creation, declaration, assignment, limitation, or extinction of any right, title, or interest in immovable property.
An instrument transferring or assigning a court decree or award that purports to create, extinguish, or affect rights in immovable property valued at ₹100 or more.
A lease deed for immovable property granted for a term exceeding one year or from year to year or reserving a yearly rent.
what_it_excludes: A will or testament, which derives its operative effect from the death of the testator and is therefore a testamentary instrument, not a non-testamentary instrument.
Any decree or order of a court (other than a compromise decree comprising immovable property not the subject of the suit), as these are excluded from compulsory registration under Section 17(2)(vi).
Any instrument relating to shares in a joint stock company, even if the company's assets consist of immovable property, as these are explicitly excluded under Section 17(2)(ii).
Any debenture issued by a joint stock company that does not itself create, declare, assign, limit or extinguish any right, title or interest in immovable property.
Any endorsement on a mortgage deed acknowledging payment of the whole or part of the mortgage money, as this is expressly excluded from compulsory registration.

A document that merely creates a right to obtain another document that will, when executed, create or affect rights in immovable property — such an agreement to sell does not itself require registration unless covered by Section 17(1A).
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a document qualifies as a non-testamentary instrument directly determines whether it attracts compulsory registration under Section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908; failure to register a compulsorily registrable non-testamentary instrument renders it inadmissible as evidence of the transaction it purports to effect and unenforceable in a court of law. It also determines the applicability of Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, for part-performance of contracts, which requires the underlying document to be a registered non-testamentary instrument.

definitions.definition: A Notary Public, for the purposes of Section 33 of the Registration Act, is an official authority empowered to execute and authenticate a power-of-attorney on behalf of a principal who does not reside in India, such authenticated power-of-attorney being recognised for the purposes of presenting documents for registration under Section 32 of the Act.
definitions.plain_english: A Notary Public is an officially appointed legal officer who has the authority to witness, certify, and authenticate important legal documents. Under the Registration Act, when an Indian property owner or party lives outside India and wants to authorise someone else to register documents on their behalf in India, they can sign a power of attorney in front of a Notary Public in the country where they are living. This authenticated document is then accepted by Indian registration offices as valid proof of authority.
real_world_examples: An Indian NRI living in the United States wishes to sell ancestral property in Mumbai. He executes a power-of-attorney before a Notary Public in New York, authorising his brother in Mumbai to register the sale deed on his behalf. The Sub-Registrar in Mumbai accepts this Notary-authenticated document under Section 33(c).

An Indian national settled in the United Kingdom needs to mortgage her flat in Bengaluru to avail a loan. She signs a power-of-attorney before a Notary Public in London, which her authorised agent presents at the local registration office in Bengaluru for registration of the mortgage deed.

A person of Indian origin residing in Canada wants to gift immovable property in Chennai to a charitable trust. He executes a power-of-attorney in front of a Canadian Notary Public, enabling a trusted friend in Chennai to appear before the Sub-Registrar and complete the registration of the gift deed.

An Indian businessman domiciled in Singapore needs to register a lease agreement for commercial property in Hyderabad. He executes a power-of-attorney authenticated by a Notary Public in Singapore, which is then produced before the registration office in Hyderabad by his appointed agent.

An Indian couple living in Dubai wish to register the sale of their jointly held agricultural land in Punjab. Both spouses execute a power-of-attorney in front of a UAE Notary Public, which their son in Punjab uses to present and register the sale deed at the local Sub-Registrar's office.
what_it_covers: A Notary Public appointed under the law of a foreign country where the principal resides, who authenticates a power-of-attorney for use in Indian registration proceedings.
Authentication by a Notary Public of a power-of-attorney executed by an Indian national or NRI residing outside India for the purpose of authorising an agent to register documents in India.

Any power-of-attorney executed before and authenticated by a Notary Public outside India, which is accepted on its face as proof of due execution without further verification, per Section 33's evidentiary rule.

A Notary Public acting in conjunction with or as an alternative to a Court, Judge, Magistrate, Indian Consul, Vice-Consul, or representative of the Central Government, all being co-equal authenticating authorities under Section 33(c).
what_it_excludes: A Notary Public as an authenticating authority for principals residing within India, where only a Registrar or Sub-Registrar (for principals in areas where the Act is in force) or a Magistrate (for principals in areas where the Act is not in force) is recognised.

Advocates, lawyers, or legal practitioners in India who may notarise documents under the Notaries Act, 1952 for domestic purposes but are not recognised under Section 33 as authorities to authenticate power-of-attorney for registration purposes when the principal resides within India.

Any authentication done by a Notary Public that pertains to documents other than a power-of-attorney, as Section 33 specifically restricts the Notary Public's recognised role to executing and authenticating powers-of-attorney for the purpose of Section 32.
Informal or self-declared notaries or commissioners for oaths who do not hold an official appointment as Notary Public under the relevant domestic law of the foreign country.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a power-of-attorney has been authenticated by a Notary Public is decisive for its recognition under Section 33(c) of the Registration Act — if the principal resides outside India and the document has not been so authenticated, the agent presenting it cannot be admitted to present or execute a document for registration under Section 32, rendering any purported registration void or liable to rejection. The validity of the entire downstream registration transaction — including sale, mortgage, lease, or gift of immovable property — depends on this authentication being properly obtained from a recognised authority such as a Notary Public.

definitions.definition: An 'officer of Government' means any person who holds an office under the Central Government or a State Government and who, in that official capacity, executes or receives instruments on behalf of the Government. As used in Section 88, such an officer is exempt from the requirement of appearing in person or by agent at a registration office for instruments executed by him or in his favour in his official capacity.
definitions.plain_english: An 'officer of Government' is any person who works in an official capacity for either the Central or a State Government. When such a person signs or receives a document as part of their official duties, the law gives them a special exemption — they do not need to personally visit or send a representative to the registration office to complete the registration process. This makes it easier for government work to continue without bureaucratic delays.
real_world_examples: A District Collector in Maharashtra executes a lease deed on behalf of the State Government for use of government land — he does not need to appear personally at the Sub-Registrar's office for registration of that instrument.

A Secretary to the Ministry of Railways, Government of India, signs a conveyance deed transferring railway land in Delhi — the document can be presented for registration without the Secretary appearing in person.

A Deputy Commissioner in Assam executes a mortgage deed in favour of the Central Government for a public infrastructure project — the officer is exempt from personal appearance at the registration office.

An Executive Engineer of a State Public Works Department in Tamil Nadu executes an agreement for acquisition of land for a highway project in his official capacity — he may have the instrument presented for registration by any prescribed manner without attending the registering office.

A Forest Department Officer in Uttarakhand executes a document granting a licence over forest land in favour of a government undertaking — the officer need not appear or sign before the registering officer as required under Section 58.
what_it_covers: Any gazetted or non-gazetted officer employed under the Central Government who executes an instrument in his official capacity.
Any State Government officer, such as a District Collector, Revenue Officer, or Secretary to Government, acting in their official role while executing or receiving a document.
Officers of government departments such as Public Works Department, Forest Department, or Revenue Department who execute instruments on behalf of the government in land or property transactions.
A government officer in whose favour an instrument is executed, where the transaction is connected to their official capacity.
what_it_excludes: Private individuals or citizens even if they are dealing with the government — the exemption is only for the government officer acting in official capacity, not the private party to the same instrument.
Public sector undertaking employees or employees of government-owned companies who are not directly officers of the Central or State Government.

An officer of Government acting in a personal or private capacity (e.g., purchasing property for himself with personal funds) — the exemption does not apply to instruments unrelated to official duties.

Administrator-General, Official Trustee, Official Assignee, Sheriff, Receiver, or Registrar of a High Court — these are separately enumerated in Section 88(1) as a distinct category and are not subsumed under 'officer of Government'.
Holders of public offices notified under Section 88(1)(d) by State Government — these are treated as a separate sub-category distinct from 'officer of Government'.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as an 'officer of Government' under Section 88 determines whether they are exempt from the mandatory requirement of personal appearance or appearance through an agent at a registration office and from signing under Section 58 — failure to comply with these requirements by a non-exempt person renders the instrument liable to be refused registration. This exemption prevents administrative paralysis in government transactions and ensures that official instruments can be registered without the physical presence of senior government functionaries.

definitions.definition: An 'order' under the Registration Act, 1908 refers to a formal direction, ruling, or decision issued by a Court, Revenue Officer, or registering authority under statutory power, which may purport or operate to create, declare, assign, limit, or extinguish any right, title, or interest in immovable property, or which directs a specific legal act such as granting a loan, vesting property, or directing registration-related compliance. Such an order may itself be a registrable instrument when it operates on immovable property rights valued at one hundred rupees or more, unless specifically exempted under the Act.
definitions.plain_english: An 'order' is an official decision or direction given by a court, a government revenue officer, or another authorised official that has a legal effect — such as transferring property rights, granting loans, or directing how property must be dealt with. Some court orders need to be registered if they create or affect property rights worth ₹100 or more. Certain orders, like those granting government loans for land improvement, are specifically exempt from registration.
real_world_examples: A Civil Court in Mumbai passes an order on a compromise decree that transfers immovable property worth ₹50 lakhs not forming part of the original suit — this order must be registered at the local Sub-Registrar's office.

A Revenue Officer in Rajasthan issues an order granting a land improvement loan to a farmer under the Land Improvement Loans Act, 1883 — this order is exempt from compulsory registration under Section 17(2)(xi).

A District Court in Delhi passes an order under the Charitable Endowments Act, 1890, vesting a trust's immovable property in the Treasurer of Charitable Endowments — this order is exempt from registration under Section 17(2)(i).

A Collector in Punjab issues an order for partition of agricultural land among co-owners — being an instrument of partition made by a Revenue Officer, it falls under the exemption in Section 17(2)(xii) and need not be registered.

A Family Court in Chennai passes an order directing transfer of a residential flat to a spouse as part of a matrimonial settlement, comprising immovable property not forming the subject-matter of the original proceeding — such an order requires registration under Section 17(1)(e).
A Sub-Registrar in Lucknow passes an order refusing to register a sale deed — the affected party can appeal this administrative order before the Registrar under Section 72 of the Act.
what_it_covers: A court order expressed to be made on a compromise that comprises immovable property other than the subject-matter of the suit, requiring compulsory registration under Section 17(1)(e).

An order of a Court or award that purports or operates to create, declare, assign, limit, or extinguish any right, title, or interest of the value of ₹100 or more in immovable property, as referred to in Section 17(1)(e).
An order passed by a registering officer such as a Sub-Registrar or Registrar under the Act refusing, accepting, or directing registration of a document, appealable under Sections 72 and 73.
An order granting a loan under the Agriculturists' Loans Act, 1884, or an order under the Land Improvement Act, 1871, which is specifically referenced as exempt from registration.
An order made under the Charitable Endowments Act, 1890, vesting or divesting property in or from a Treasurer of Charitable Endowments.
what_it_excludes: A decree or order of a Court that does not comprise or affect immovable property, as it carries no registration obligation under the Act.
A court order not expressed to be on a compromise and relating only to property already forming the subject-matter of the suit — expressly excluded under Section 17(2)(vi).

An order granting a loan under the Land Improvement Loans Act, 1883, or the Agriculturists' Loans Act, 1884, which is explicitly exempted from compulsory registration under Section 17(2)(xi) and (xii).
A certificate of sale granted to a purchaser of property sold by public auction by a Civil or Revenue Officer — specifically excluded from compulsory registration under Section 17(2)(iii).
An internal administrative circular or executive instruction issued by a government department that does not create, declare, assign, limit, or extinguish any right, title, or interest in property.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a document qualifies as a registrable 'order' determines whether it must be compulsorily registered under Section 17 — failure to register a registrable order renders it inadmissible as evidence of the transaction it affects and incapable of conferring property rights. Conversely, if an order falls within an express exemption, registration is not required and the order operates validly without it.

Such an order may itself be a registrable instrument when it operates on immovable property rights valued at one hundred rupees or more, unless specifically exempted under the Act.

Examples: A Civil Court in Mumbai passes an order on a compromise decree that transfers immovable property worth ₹50 lakhs not forming part of the original suit — this order must be registered at the local Sub-Registrar's office. | A Revenue Officer in Rajasthan issues an order granting a land improvement loan to a farmer under the Land Improvement Loans Act, 1883 — this order is exempt from compulsory registration under Section 17(2)(xi). | A District Court in Delhi passes an order under the Charitable Endowments Act, 1890, vesting a trust's immovable property in the Treasurer of Charitable Endowments — this order is exempt from registration under Section 17(2)(i). | A Collector in Punjab issues an order for partition of agricultural land among co-owners — being an instrument of partition made by a Revenue Officer, it falls under the exemption in Section 17(2)(xii) and need not be registered. | A Family Court in Chennai passes an order directing transfer of a residential flat to a spouse as part of a matrimonial settlement, comprising immovable property not forming the subject-matter of the original proceeding — such an order requires registration under Section 17(1)(e). | A Sub-Registrar in Lucknow passes an order refusing to register a sale deed — the affected party can appeal this administrative order before the Registrar under Section 72 of the Act.

definitions.definition: A 'plan' under the Registration Act refers to a graphical or diagrammatic representation of immovable property contained in or accompanying a non-testamentary document, depicting the layout, boundaries, dimensions, or spatial arrangement of such property. Where a document contains a plan of any property comprised therein, it must be accompanied by a true copy of the plan for registration purposes, and such copy is filed in Book No. 1 upon completion of registration.
definitions.plain_english: A 'plan' is a drawn diagram or layout sketch of a piece of land or property that is attached to or included in a legal document being registered. It visually shows the shape, size, and boundaries of the property being dealt with. When a document contains such a plan, an exact copy of it must be submitted along with the document at the time of registration. This copy is kept permanently in the official record books of the registration office.
real_world_examples: A developer in Pune attaches a detailed site plan showing plot dimensions and boundary walls to a sale deed for a residential flat; a true copy of this plan must be submitted to the Sub-Registrar's office along with the deed for registration under Section 21.

A landowner in rural Tamil Nadu executes a partition deed dividing agricultural land among siblings, attaching a surveyed plan showing each share's extent and boundaries; the registering officer requires a true copy of this plan to be filed in Book No. 1.

A builder in Delhi registers a lease deed for commercial premises in a multi-storey complex and includes an architectural plan indicating the leased floor area and demarcated zones; the Sub-Registrar retains a copy of the plan as part of the registered record.

A property situated across two revenue districts in Maharashtra is the subject of a mortgage deed accompanied by a cadastral plan; the Sub-Registrar forwards copies of both the document and the plan to the Registrar of the other district as required under Section 65.

A cooperative housing society in Kolkata registers a conveyance deed for a plot showing internal road layouts and open spaces via an attached plan; the registration is complete only after the true copy of the plan is filed in the register-book.

An NRI selling ancestral property in Kerala includes a Government survey-based plan with the sale deed; the Registrar, while forwarding copies under Section 66, also sends the copy of the plan to every other Registrar in whose district any part of the property is situate.
what_it_covers: A diagrammatic layout or site plan attached to a sale deed depicting the boundaries, dimensions, and orientation of the property being transferred.
A surveyed or architectural plan included in a lease or mortgage deed showing the demarcated area of the immovable property concerned.
A cadastral or Government survey-based plan accompanying a document where the property spans multiple districts, requiring multiple true copies equal to the number of such districts.
Any sketch, drawing, or graphical representation of immovable property that is part of or referred to in a non-testamentary document presented for registration.
A plan forwarded by a Sub-Registrar or Registrar to other registration offices under Sections 65 and 66 as part of inter-district registration compliance.
what_it_excludes: A purely verbal or written description of property boundaries contained in the document body, which constitutes a description under Section 21 but not a 'plan' requiring a true copy.

A Government map or survey referenced in the document but not physically contained in or annexed to the document itself, as only maps or plans 'contained' in the document trigger the true copy requirement.
Testamentary documents such as wills that contain property sketches, since the true copy requirement under Section 21 applies only to non-testamentary documents.
A rough or informal hand-drawn sketch made informally by parties outside the document that is not formally annexed to or made part of the document presented for registration.
Photographs or satellite imagery of the property, which do not constitute a 'plan' in the diagrammatic or cartographic sense contemplated by the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: If a non-testamentary document containing a plan is presented for registration without an accompanying true copy of the plan, the registering officer is obligated to refuse acceptance of the document under Section 21, rendering the registration incomplete and the document unregistered. Compliance with the plan-copy requirement is also essential for the proper filing in Book No. 1 and for inter-district forwarding obligations under Sections 61, 65, and 66, affecting the enforceability and public notice function of the registered document.

definitions.definition: A power of attorney, within the meaning of the Registration Act, is a written instrument by which a person executing or claiming under a document, or their representative or assign, duly authorises an agent to present that document for registration on their behalf, such instrument being executed and authenticated in the manner prescribed under the Act.
definitions.plain_english: A power of attorney is a written document through which a person gives another person the legal authority to act on their behalf for a specific purpose — in this context, to present a document for registration at the registration office. It must be properly signed and verified in the way the law requires. Without this authorisation, only the person directly involved in the transaction can present the document for registration.
real_world_examples: A property seller in Mumbai who is residing in the United States executes a power of attorney in favour of his brother in India, authorising him to present the sale deed to the Sub-Registrar's office for registration on his behalf.

An elderly woman in Chennai who is unable to travel due to illness grants a power of attorney to her daughter, permitting her to appear before the registering officer and present a gift deed for registration.

A corporate company in Delhi, which is a party to a lease agreement, authorises its legal manager through a power of attorney to present the registered lease document at the proper registration office on behalf of the company.

A non-resident Indian living in London executes a power of attorney before the Indian Consul, authorising a trusted friend in Bengaluru to present a mortgage deed for registration at the local Sub-Registrar's office.

A person who has purchased agricultural land in Pune but is stationed in a remote area for military duty grants a power of attorney to his advocate to handle all registration formalities for the sale deed on his behalf.
what_it_covers: A written instrument executed by a person who is a party to a document being registered, authorising a named agent to present that document at the proper registration office on their behalf.
A power of attorney executed by the representative or assign of the person executing or claiming under the document, delegating the task of registration to an agent.
A power of attorney executed abroad before an Indian Consul or other prescribed authority, enabling NRIs to authorise a local agent to complete registration formalities in India.
An instrument of authorisation executed by a corporate entity or body through its authorised signatory, appointing an agent to present documents for registration.
A power of attorney authenticated by a Notary Public or other competent authority as prescribed under the Act, enabling the agent to legally represent the principal before the registering officer.
what_it_excludes: An oral or informal authorisation or verbal instruction given by one person to another to present a document for registration — the power of attorney must be in writing and duly authenticated.
A general or unstamped authorisation letter that has not been executed and authenticated in the manner prescribed under the Registration Act and allied rules.
Direct personal appearance by the executing party themselves, which does not require any power of attorney and falls under the primary mode of presentation under Section 32.

Documents presented under Sections 31, 88, and 89, which involve special provisions for registration outside the registration office or by public officers, and do not require presentation through a power-of-attorney-authorised agent in the ordinary sense.
An authority to adopt or a will being presented by a person who is not the agent of the executing party but claims in their own right under the document.
definitions.why_it_matters: A document presented for registration by a person other than the executing party is valid only if that person holds a duly executed and authenticated power of attorney — failing which, the registering officer is legally bound to refuse registration, rendering the document unregistered and potentially unenforceable against third parties. The requirement ensures accountability and prevents fraudulent or unauthorised presentation of documents at the registration office.

definitions.definition: A 'power to adopt' refers to the legal authority conferred by a registered instrument upon a person to adopt a child on behalf of another, particularly a widow or other individual authorised by a husband or donor to make such adoption. Under Section 49 of the Registration Act, 1908, no document conferring a power to adopt shall be effective or received as evidence unless it has been duly registered.
definitions.plain_english: A 'power to adopt' is the legal permission given to someone, usually a wife or another trusted person, to adopt a child on behalf of someone else — for example, a husband who may be dying or unable to adopt himself. This permission must be written in a document and that document must be officially registered with the Registration office to be legally valid. Without registration, neither the permission nor the adoption carried out under it will be recognised by courts.
real_world_examples: A Hindu man in Rajasthan, on his deathbed, executes a written document authorising his wife to adopt a son from his brother's family after his death. This document must be registered under the Registration Act for the wife to validly exercise the power to adopt.

A landlord in Tamil Nadu executes a deed granting his childless widowed daughter-in-law the authority to adopt a male child to continue the family lineage. The deed is presented before a Sub-Registrar in Chennai and duly registered, making the power to adopt legally enforceable.

A man in Varanasi tries to adopt a nephew after his wife exercises an unregistered 'power to adopt' document. The adoptive family disputes the adoption in court, and the court refuses to admit the unregistered document as evidence of the power to adopt under Section 49.

A Hindu joint family elder in Maharashtra executes a registered instrument granting his younger brother's wife the power to adopt a child in the absence of the elder brother, who is posted abroad. The registered document is later used in a succession dispute to prove the legality of the adopted child's claim to ancestral property.

A woman in Kolkata claims inheritance for her adopted son, citing a power to adopt given to her by her late husband. When the document is found to be unregistered, the court holds that it cannot confer any valid power to adopt and the adoption is declared void for lack of evidence.
what_it_covers: A written instrument executed by a Hindu husband authorising his wife to adopt a child on his behalf after his death or during incapacity.
A registered deed conferring on a widow or other authorised person the legal power to select and adopt a child to continue the family line.
Any document, required to be registered under Section 17, that expressly grants someone the authority to complete an adoption transaction on behalf of the donor.
A power to adopt exercised by an agent or representative under a registered instrument, used in Hindu adoption proceedings governed by the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956.
what_it_excludes: An unregistered document purporting to grant power to adopt — such a document cannot confer any valid power to adopt or be used as evidence of such power in court proceedings.
A verbal or oral grant of authority to adopt a child, which cannot constitute a legally enforceable 'power to adopt' under the Registration Act framework.

A general power of attorney that does not expressly or specifically confer the authority to adopt a child, as it would not fall within the specific meaning of 'power to adopt' for registration purposes.
Documents relating to guardianship or custody of a minor that do not involve the formal legal transfer of parental rights through adoption.
definitions.why_it_matters: If a document conferring a power to adopt is not registered, it is rendered legally void and cannot be admitted as evidence in any court proceeding under Section 49 of the Registration Act, 1908, which means any adoption purportedly made under such unregistered authority has no legal standing. This directly affects the adopted child's right to inherit property, claim succession, and establish legal status within the family, and the absence of registration blocks all legal remedies premised on such adoption.

definitions.definition: A power-of-attorney, for the purposes of Section 32 of the Registration Act, is a document executed by a principal authorising an agent to present a document for registration on the principal's behalf, which must be executed before and authenticated by the Registrar or Sub-Registrar within whose district or sub-district the principal resides (if residing in a part of India where the Act is in force), by any Magistrate (if residing in a part of India where the Act is not in force), or by a Notary Public, Court, Judge, Magistrate, Indian Consul, Vice-Consul, or representative of the Central Government (if the principal resides outside India).
definitions.plain_english: A power-of-attorney is a written document in which one person (the principal) gives another person (the agent) the legal authority to act on their behalf — in this case, to present documents for registration. For it to be valid under the Registration Act, it must be officially authenticated by the right authority depending on where the principal lives. For example, if you live in Delhi, you would sign the power-of-attorney in front of the local Registrar or Sub-Registrar.
real_world_examples: A property owner living in Mumbai who wants their brother in Pune to register a sale deed on their behalf executes a power-of-attorney before the Sub-Registrar of their Mumbai sub-district, authorising the brother to present the sale deed at the Pune registration office.

An Indian citizen temporarily residing in a state governed by a different property law (e.g., Jammu & Kashmir prior to reorganisation) executes a power-of-attorney before a local Magistrate to authorise an agent to register a deed of mortgage in a state where the Registration Act applies.

An NRI living in the United States wishes to sell ancestral property in Chennai; they execute a power-of-attorney before a Notary Public in New York or the Indian Consul/Vice-Consul, which is then used by their relative in Chennai to present the sale deed for registration.

A person confined in Tihar Jail in Delhi who needs to register a gift deed in their favour authorises an agent through a power-of-attorney attested by the Sub-Registrar who visits the jail premises, without requiring the prisoner's personal attendance at the registration office.

An elderly person in Hyderabad who is bedridden and unable to attend the registration office executes a power-of-attorney at their home, with the Registrar or Sub-Registrar visiting and attesting the document after satisfying themselves that the execution is voluntary.
An Indian diplomat posted abroad executes a power-of-attorney before a Judge of a foreign court or an Indian Consul to authorise their spouse to register a housing loan mortgage deed in Bengaluru.

what_it_excludes: A power-of-attorney not authenticated by the specific authorities prescribed under Section 33 (e.g., one merely notarised by a private advocate or attested by a general witness), which will not be recognised for the purposes of Section 32.

A power-of-attorney executed by a principal residing in a part of India where the Act is in force but authenticated before a Magistrate instead of the Registrar or Sub-Registrar of the relevant district or sub-district.

definitions.why_it_matters: Only a power-of-attorney recognised under Section 33 can be used by an agent to present a document for registration on behalf of the principal under Section 32; if the power-of-attorney does not meet these requirements, the agent lacks legal authority to present the document and the registration will be refused or deemed invalid, potentially rendering the underlying transaction unenforceable. This directly determines whether a registered document achieves legal validity and whether obligations such as stamp duty payment and compulsory registration under the Act are properly discharged.

definitions.definition: A 'Presidency-town' refers to the municipal area of a former Presidency city in India — namely Kolkata (formerly Calcutta), Mumbai (formerly Bombay), or Chennai (formerly Madras) — which historically constituted the headquarters of a British Presidency and continues to be recognised as a distinct administrative and jurisdictional category under the Registration Act, 1908. A district including a Presidency-town is subject to a special administrative regime distinct from ordinary districts, particularly with respect to the appointment of a substitute Registrar during absence or vacancy.
definitions.plain_english: A 'Presidency-town' is one of the three major historic cities in India — Mumbai, Kolkata, or Chennai — that were the capitals of the old British Presidencies. These cities are treated as a special category under the registration law because of their unique administrative history. When the Registrar of a district that includes one of these cities is absent, only the Inspector-General (and not the local District Court Judge) can appoint a replacement.
real_world_examples: The Registrar of a district covering Mumbai city goes on unexpected medical leave; under Section 10, only the Inspector-General of Registration (Maharashtra) can appoint an acting Registrar, unlike in an ordinary district where the District Judge could step in.

A property document is presented for registration at the Kolkata district registration office, but the Registrar's post falls vacant mid-month; the State Government or Inspector-General must fill the gap through the special Presidency-town procedure rather than the general district procedure.

In Chennai, when the Registrar of the district encompassing the Presidency-town is on deputation, the Inspector-General of Registration (Tamil Nadu) appoints a temporary Registrar to ensure uninterrupted document registration services.

A citizen attempting to register a lease deed in a South Mumbai sub-district office finds the Registrar absent; the legal challenge over who has authority to appoint a replacement is resolved by applying the Presidency-town rule under Section 10 — exclusively through the Inspector-General.

A court case in Kolkata questions the validity of documents registered during a period when a District Judge (instead of the Inspector-General) had purported to appoint a temporary Registrar for the Presidency-town district, leading to scrutiny under the special rule of Section 10.
what_it_covers: The municipal and administrative area of Mumbai (formerly Bombay), being the seat of the former Bombay Presidency.
The municipal and administrative area of Kolkata (formerly Calcutta), being the seat of the former Bengal Presidency.
The municipal and administrative area of Chennai (formerly Madras), being the seat of the former Madras Presidency.
Any district whose territorial limits include or encompass one of these three historic Presidency cities, thereby attracting the special appointment procedure under Section 10.
what_it_excludes: Ordinary revenue or registration districts that do not include a former British Presidency capital, such as Pune, Hyderabad, or Bengaluru.
State capital cities that were not historical British Presidencies, such as Lucknow, Bhopal, or Patna, even if they are major metropolitan centres.
Sub-districts or talukas within Presidency-town districts — the special rule applies specifically to the Registrar of the district, not to Sub-Registrars operating within such districts.
Union Territories and newly created administrative districts that have no historical connection to the three original British Presidencies.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of a district as one 'including a Presidency-town' determines whether the District Court Judge has any authority to appoint a temporary Registrar during absence or vacancy — in Presidency-town districts, that power is reserved exclusively for the Inspector-General, making any appointment by a District Judge legally invalid and potentially rendering documents registered during such a period liable to challenge. Failure to follow the correct appointment procedure could compromise the legal validity and evidentiary value of registered documents executed during the period of absence.

definitions.definition: A 'proceeding' under the Registration Act, 1908 refers to any formal legal or judicial process before a court, tribunal, or authority, including suits, applications, or actions, in the course of which a decree or order may be made that purports or operates to create, declare, assign, limit, or extinguish any right, title, or interest in immovable property. The term is used in the context of Section 82 to denote official proceedings in which penal consequences for false statements or fraudulent conduct are attracted, and in Section 17 to distinguish the subject-matter of a suit or proceeding from property included by compromise.
definitions.plain_english: A 'proceeding' means any official legal process or action that takes place before a court or a registration authority. This includes lawsuits, formal applications, or any other official steps taken as part of the registration or legal system. In simpler terms, it is any formal step in a legal or administrative process where decisions about property or documents are made.
real_world_examples: A civil suit filed in a District Court in Mumbai over ownership of a flat, during which the court passes a compromise decree including additional immovable property not originally part of the suit — such a proceeding attracts mandatory registration under Section 17.

A proceeding before a Sub-Registrar in Delhi where a party is found to have made a false declaration to obtain registration of a sale deed — the Sub-Registrar initiates action under Section 82 for the false statement made in the course of that proceeding.

A revenue proceeding before a Tehsildar in Uttar Pradesh where a partition order is made affecting agricultural land — the order arising from this proceeding may require registration depending on its nature.

An application made before the Registrar in Chennai seeking registration of a court decree that includes immovable property beyond the original subject-matter of the suit, triggering the question of whether such a proceeding's outcome is compulsorily registrable.

A proceeding under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code before the National Company Law Tribunal in Kolkata, where an order transferring immovable property is passed, raising questions about registration obligations under the Registration Act.
semantic_tags: decree or order arising from proceeding
what_it_covers: Civil suits before a District Court or High Court in which a decree or order relating to immovable property is passed, including compromise decrees that include property beyond the original suit subject-matter.

Formal proceedings before a registering officer or Sub-Registrar under the Registration Act, during which parties make declarations or produce documents, and in which penalties under Section 82 may be attracted for false statements.
Revenue proceedings before competent authorities such as a Tehsildar or Revenue Officer where orders affecting land or immovable property rights are made.
Applications and hearings before a Registrar regarding the opening of deposited wills or other documents, constituting proceedings in the administrative sense of the Act.
Any judicial proceeding before a Magistrate or court that results in an award, order, or decree purporting to affect rights in immovable property.
what_it_excludes: Informal negotiations or private settlements between parties that are not conducted before any court, tribunal, or authority, and which do not result in any official order or decree.
A mere filing or presentation of a document for registration that has not yet been acted upon or examined by the registering officer, as this does not constitute a formal proceeding.
Administrative correspondence or communications between parties and a registration office that do not amount to a hearing, inquiry, or examination before a competent authority.
Testamentary proceedings related solely to the deposit of a sealed will under Section 42, where no inquiry into property rights or false statements is involved.
Purely ministerial or clerical acts by a registration officer, such as issuing certified copies of registered documents, which do not involve adjudication or formal process.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act or process qualifies as a 'proceeding' determines whether Section 82 penalties for making false statements or producing false documents apply, exposing a party to criminal liability for perjury or fraud before a registering authority. Additionally, the characterisation of an outcome as arising from a 'proceeding' determines whether the resulting decree or order requires compulsory registration under Section 17, affecting the enforceability and validity of property rights.

definitions.definition: The 'proper officer' means the registering officer duly empowered and authorised under the Registration Act to receive and accept documents for registration within his territorial and subject-matter jurisdiction. It refers to the Sub-Registrar or Registrar before whom a document must be presented for registration in accordance with the provisions of the Act.
definitions.plain_english: The 'proper officer' is the government official — usually a Sub-Registrar or Registrar — who is legally authorised to accept and register documents in a specific area. When you want to register a property sale deed, a lease agreement, or any other document requiring registration, you must go to this specific officer at the correct registration office. Presenting a document to any other official or office would not count as valid registration under the law.
real_world_examples: A buyer and seller in Pune complete a sale deed for a flat. They must present the document to the Sub-Registrar of the sub-district where the property is located within four months of signing — that Sub-Registrar is the 'proper officer' for this registration.

A landlord in Chennai executes a ten-year commercial lease agreement. The proper officer before whom the lease must be presented for registration is the Sub-Registrar having jurisdiction over the locality where the leased premises are situated.

A gift deed executed in Delhi for immovable property must be presented to the Sub-Registrar of the relevant sub-district in Delhi. Presenting it to a revenue officer or a magistrate would not satisfy the requirement of presentation to the 'proper officer' under Section 23.

When a civil court in Kolkata issues a decree for specific performance and the decreeing party wishes to register a certified copy, they must present it to the Sub-Registrar of the appropriate registration district within four months — that Sub-Registrar is the proper officer for the purpose.

A power of attorney executed in Mumbai authorising someone to sell agricultural land in Nagpur must be presented to the Sub-Registrar with jurisdiction over Nagpur, who is the proper officer, and not to any official in Mumbai.
what_it_covers: A Sub-Registrar duly appointed and empowered under the Registration Act to register non-testamentary documents in a specific sub-district.
A Registrar acting within his jurisdiction to accept documents that fall under his registration authority as prescribed by the Act.
A Joint Sub-Registrar or any officer specifically empowered to perform registration functions in the absence of or in addition to the regular Sub-Registrar.
An Indian Consul authorised to perform registration functions for documents executed abroad by Indian nationals, to the extent empowered under the Act.
what_it_excludes: A revenue officer or patwari who may deal with land records but has no authority under the Registration Act to accept documents for registration.
A notary public who may attest or certify documents but is not empowered to register documents under the Registration Act.
A civil court judge or magistrate who, though a judicial officer, is not designated as a registering officer and cannot accept documents for registration purposes.
An ordinary government servant or officer of government who is not specifically appointed or empowered under the Registration Act to perform registration functions.
A private advocate or legal professional before whom a document may be executed or attested but who has no registration authority under the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Presentation of a document to anyone other than the 'proper officer' within the four-month period prescribed by Section 23 renders the document incapable of valid registration, potentially making it inadmissible as evidence of the transaction it purports to record. The identity of the proper officer directly determines whether the time-limit obligation under Section 23 is satisfied and whether the document achieves its registered status with the legal consequences that flow from registration.

definitions.definition: The 'proper registration fee' means the fee lawfully chargeable and payable for the registration of a document under the Registration Act, as prescribed by the applicable fee schedule or rules, against which fines for delay or default are calculated and measured under the Act.
definitions.plain_english: The 'proper registration fee' is the official, standard fee that a person must pay to get a document legally registered at the registration office. It is the baseline amount set by law for registering a particular type of document. Fines imposed for late or irregular registration are calculated as multiples of this fee, making it a key reference point for penalty computation.
real_world_examples: A property buyer in Mumbai who fails to appear before the Sub-Registrar within the prescribed time for registering a sale deed must pay a fine of up to ten times the proper registration fee (e.g., if the registration fee is ₹30,000, the fine can be up to ₹3,00,000) before the Registrar can direct registration of the document.

In Delhi, when a gift deed for immovable property is presented four months late due to the donor's hospitalisation, the Registrar calculates the permissible fine by referring to the proper registration fee schedule applicable to gift deeds, and levies a fine not exceeding ten times that amount.

A landlord in Chennai who approaches the Registrar under the proviso to Section 34 for late registration of a lease agreement is informed that the fine will be computed as a multiple of the proper registration fee prescribed for lease documents under the Tamil Nadu Registration Fee Rules.

The Inspector-General of Registration in Karnataka, exercising powers under Section 70, remits the excess amount between a fine levied under Section 34 and the proper registration fee for a mortgage deed, providing financial relief to a farmer who had missed the registration deadline due to floods.

In Kolkata, a company seeking to register a debenture deed after the stipulated period pays a fine calculated at five times the proper registration fee as directed by the Registrar, with the proper registration fee serving as the statutory measuring unit for the penalty imposed.
what_it_covers: The standard fee prescribed under the applicable fee schedule or rules for registering any non-testamentary document such as a sale deed, mortgage deed, lease, gift deed, or power of attorney.

The fee amount used as the multiplier base for computing fines under the proviso to Section 34 where persons executing a document fail to appear before the registering officer within the prescribed time.

The reference amount used by the Inspector-General under Section 70 to determine how much of a fine levied under Section 25 or Section 34 may be remitted, being the difference between the fine and this fee.
Fees chargeable for registration of documents relating to immovable property, movable property, or other registrable instruments as set out in the State Government's prescribed fee schedule.
what_it_excludes: Penalty amounts or fines themselves — the proper registration fee is the base fee only and does not include the additional fine imposed for delay or default under Section 25 or Section 34.

Incidental or ancillary charges such as copying fees, search fees, endorsement fees, or administrative service charges levied by the registration office that are not part of the prescribed registration fee.

Fees payable in respect of documents exempted from registration fees under any law or government notification, such as certain government instruments or documents executed by or in favour of the government.
Any voluntary or negotiated payment made outside the statutory fee schedule, as the 'proper' registration fee is strictly the legally prescribed amount and not any informal or excess payment.
definitions.why_it_matters: The proper registration fee is the statutory benchmark against which all fines for delayed or irregular appearance under Section 34 are computed — without establishing this figure, neither the Registrar can direct conditional registration nor can the Inspector-General lawfully remit fines under Section 70. Incorrect determination of this fee directly affects the validity of the fine levied and the legality of the registration itself.

definitions.definition: The 'proper registration office' means the registration office before which a document is required to be presented for registration under the provisions of the Registration Act, being the office of the Registrar or Sub-Registrar within whose jurisdiction or sub-district the property to which the document relates is situated or the transaction is deemed to have taken place, as determined by the applicable provisions of the Act.
definitions.plain_english: The 'proper registration office' is the specific government registration office where you must go to officially register a document — it is not just any registration office, but the one that has jurisdiction over the area where the property or transaction is located. For example, if you are buying a flat in Pune, you must go to the Sub-Registrar's office that covers that particular area of Pune. Going to the wrong office means your document cannot be validly registered there.
real_world_examples: A buyer and seller of agricultural land in Nashik district must present their sale deed at the Sub-Registrar's office of the sub-district in Nashik where the land is situated — this is the proper registration office for that transaction, and no other office will accept the document for registration.

A person executing a lease agreement for a commercial property in Bengaluru's Jayanagar locality must present the document at the Sub-Registrar's office having jurisdiction over Jayanagar, not at any other Sub-Registrar's office in Bengaluru city.

When a property owner in Kolkata's South 24 Parganas district gifts immovable property to a family member, the gift deed must be presented at the proper registration office — the Sub-Registrar's office covering the specific area in South 24 Parganas — where the gifted property is located.

An NRI selling a flat in Mumbai's Bandra suburb through a power-of-attorney holder must ensure that the authorised agent presents the sale document at the Sub-Registrar's office with jurisdiction over Bandra, as that is the proper registration office, and the photograph and fingerprints of both buyer and seller must be affixed there as required under Section 32A.

A developer in Hyderabad executing a construction agreement linked to transfer of immovable property must present the document before the Sub-Registrar's office corresponding to the locality where the property is situated, making that office the 'proper registration office' obligating compliance with photograph and fingerprint requirements under Section 32A.
what_it_covers: The Sub-Registrar's office having territorial jurisdiction over the sub-district in which the immovable property subject to the document is situated, where sale deeds, gift deeds, or mortgage documents must be presented.

The Registrar's office having jurisdiction over documents or transactions that fall within the Registrar's competence under the Registration Act, including documents that cannot be registered by a Sub-Registrar.

The registration office designated under the Act before which both the presenting party and, in case of property transfers, the buyer and seller must appear and affix their photographs and fingerprints as mandated by Section 32A.

Any registration office — whether of a Registrar or Sub-Registrar — specifically empowered and geographically competent under the Registration Act to accept and process a particular document for registration.
what_it_excludes: Any registration office that lacks territorial or subject-matter jurisdiction over the document being presented, even if it is a valid Sub-Registrar or Registrar office elsewhere in the same State.
Revenue offices, survey offices, or other government offices that may deal with land records but are not designated registration offices under the Registration Act.
Offices of Notary Publics, stamp vendors, or other document-attesting authorities that are not empowered to register documents under the Registration Act.

An Indian Consul's office or Vice-Consul's office abroad, which may handle certain registration functions under the Act but would not constitute the 'proper registration office' for documents relating to immovable property situated within India requiring presentation under Section 32.
definitions.why_it_matters: Presenting a document at an office that is not the 'proper registration office' renders the registration invalid, meaning the document cannot confer, declare, or extinguish any right in immovable property as against third parties. Non-compliance with Section 32A requirements — including affixing photographs and fingerprints at the proper registration office — may result in the registering officer refusing to register the document, making any purported transfer of immovable property legally ineffective.
